title: 3DIVART - 3D Interactive Visual Art
content:
Ray-Tracing Meets Auto-Stereoscopy

3DIVART is my attempt to adapt ray-tracing and ray-marching shaders from locations such as ShaderToy for use on auto-stereoscopic screens using Tao3D.

Result

3D interactive visual art—something that you see in 3D, but that is perfectly synthetic. Art that exists only in the mathematics of the rendering algorithms.

Techniques

Ray-Marching: Highly detailed rendering technique which can compute:

  • Realistic shadows
  • Complex lighting
  • Scenes with a very large number of visible elements
  • Real-time on GPU

Interactive Elements: Unlike static shader demos, these pieces are interactive, responding to user input and running in true stereoscopic 3D on specialized displays.

Sources

Most 3DIVART pieces are obviously derived from work on ShaderToy, but I also started creating a few pieces of my own, exploring the intersection of:

  • Mathematical beauty
  • Real-time rendering
  • Stereoscopic display
  • Interactive art

Philosophy

Exploring strange forms of art at the intersection of technology and visual experience. Creating experiences that can only exist in the digital realm.

title: Alpha Waves / Continuum
content:
First 3D Platform Game Ever

Alpha-Waves was the first 3D platform game ever created. I started working on it in 1988, and it was published by Infogrames in 1990.

Gameplay

A puzzle/labyrinth game where you jumped from platform to platform to reach doors giving access to the next room.

Innovation

In my opinion, the first truly immersive 3D game, combining:

  • True 6-axis 3D movement
  • Physics engine (primitive but effective)
  • Interaction with a large number of objects
  • Fully 3D environment

Genesis & Technology

Its genesis, technology, and references to games of the same era are all documented on my blog. I published the source code for archeologists interested in obsolete technologies.

Recognition

Tamaracade published a really good video on the topic, and it's documented on Wikipedia as a milestone in gaming history.

Modern Port

At some point between jobs, I rewrote Alpha Waves in C to play it on modern machines. The new job caught up before I could finish the port, but the project is available on SourceForge.

Quote: "Playing the game was a surreal experience. I was remembering it all today." - Anonymous player review

Quote: "Christophe is an open minded entrepreneur" - P. Zucchetta on the Continuum project

title: DB48X - Modern RPL Calculator
content:
A Modern Implementation of Reverse Polish Lisp

The DB48X project intends to rebuild and improve the user experience of the HP48 family of calculators, notably their "Reverse Polish Lisp" (RPL) language with its rich set of data types and built-in functions, and Lisp-level programming power.

Target Platforms

The project presently targets the SwissMicro DM42 and DM32 calculators, leveraging their built-in software platform known as DMCP. There is also a simulator tested on macOS and Linux.

Long-term Vision

Port DB48X to various physical calculator platforms:

  • ARM-based HP50 and related machines (HP49, HP48Gii)
  • HP Prime (at least the G1 model)
  • Other calculator platforms

Presentation

This project was presented at FOSDEM in 2023 and an update was given in 2024, showcasing the modern approach to calculator programming.

Heritage

Building on decades of calculator programming experience, from the original HPDS development system to this modern reimplementation of RPL.

title: HP ECUTEST Real-Time System
content:
Real-Time Automotive Testing

HP ECUTEST was a real-time test system for car electronics, particularly engine control units (ECU).

Capabilities

  • Generated or monitored several hundred signals (~400 typical)
  • Wide variety of analog and digital devices
  • Sub-millisecond closed loop (250µs in some configurations)
  • Continuous data logging with multiple time bases
  • Some based on time, some based on engine rotation

Operating System Design

The ECUTEST operating system featured:

  • Heterogeneous multiprocessing: x86 Windows PC + real-time boards
  • Real-time boards: 68040 running pSOS or PA-RISC with HP-RT
  • Distributed device driver model:
    • Configuration by controlling PC
    • Real-time measurements on 68040/PA-RISC
    • Disk I/O for data logging on PC
  • VME or VXI devices with their own CPUs (68040 or 68332)

Hardware-Agnostic Binary Translator

Included a unique feature: customers could specify equations computed every cycle, independent of the underlying hardware architecture.

Scale Evolution

ECUTEST Lite: Half the size of the original (which was refrigerator-sized), most of the testing capabilities, using VME instead of the more expensive VXI.

Manufacturing Release: A major milestone celebrated with team cartoons capturing the journey of wild optimism, tight hardware fits, union workers at demos, ever-changing product structure, and the memorable "Yes, it's a bit slow to start" moment when we went to lunch waiting for the software to launch!

title: Emacs on Aqua
content:
First Graphical Emacs on macOS

When Apple released macOS with only a text-only version of Emacs (working only in Terminal app), I was disappointed.

Taking Initiative

I waited a couple of months, thinking someone else would fix this. But it didn't happen. So I:

  • Took an old NeXT port
  • Adapted it to the Aqua graphical interface
  • Added macOS-only niceties like transparent windows
  • Published it on SourceForge

Impact

This port provided the first graphical Emacs experience on macOS Aqua, filling an important gap for Mac-using developers who relied on Emacs.

Legacy

By the time Emacs 23 was out, there were several forks and alternative implementations. Soon, maintaining a separate branch became unnecessary, since the primary version had integrated native graphical support for macOS.

This port is now obsolete, but it served its purpose: getting Emacs users productive on the new macOS platform while the official port caught up.

Philosophy

An example of: "If nobody else will fix it, maybe I should."

title: HP-48 Calculator Games & HPDS
content:
Viral Games & Development System

Created HPDS (HP Development System) and several viral games for HP-48 calculators.

HPDS - HP Development System

Evolution from SATAS (assembler for HP-28C, HP-28S, HP-48SX) into a complete development system for HP calculators. Used to create numerous programs and games.

PacMan for HP48 - First Viral Calculator Game

Innovation: First use of HP48 hardware scroll

Released initially as an assembly-only program with HPDS 1.0, later converted to HP-48 library with HPDS 2.0 in 1991. According to Paul Courbis, this was the first game to use the hardware scroll of the HP-48 calculator, making the game very fluid.

Viral Spread: Being one of the very first games for the HP-48, PacMan quickly became popular, taking advantage of the HP48's built-in infrared networking to spread virally—hopping from machine to machine, spreading to other countries including the United States. I received letters from all over the world.

Tetris for HP48 - Tutorial Game

Demo game for HPDS written in 1991. A simple Tetris clone intended primarily as a tutorial and demo for what could be done with a cross-development tool for HP48.

Lemmings for HP48 - Pushing the Envelope

Ambition: Version 3.0 of HPDS included a clone of Lemmings, complete with an editor to create new levels. Source code dated from 1993.

Technical Challenge: Pushed the limits of the calculator in memory and in the number of lemmings animated on screen with a meager 2MHz 4-bit CPU.

Space Invaders - The Game I Never Wrote

Someone wrote a Space Invaders game and put my name in the credits! A friend said "Your Space Invaders is really not as good as your other games." I had never written it. I'm still hoping it was a kind of homage to my other games. I never knew who the real author was.

Quote: "The first games to use the HP-48 hardware scroll" - P. Courbis on viral calculator games

title: HP aC++ Compiler & C++ ABI
content:
Industry-Wide C++ Standard Implementation

At Hewlett-Packard's Compiler and Languages Lab in Cupertino, California, I made fundamental contributions to C++ compiler technology that are still used today.

HP aC++ Compiler Work

Working on the aC++ compiler (from Taligent codebase):

  • Templates implementation and optimization
  • Performance improvements
  • Run-time library development
  • Precompiled headers
  • Exception handling
  • Represented HP at C++ standards committee

Revolutionary Exception Handling

Traditional exception handling was hostile to optimizations—a real problem for processors like Itanium where compiler optimizations were essential for performance.

Implemented a new approach designed by brilliant HP minds that:

  • Allowed aggressive compiler optimizations
  • Maintained full C++ exception semantics
  • Became the standard approach in modern compilers
  • Documented in an IEEE article

Quote: "An exceedingly sharp engineer" - Mark Mitchell

C++ ABI - Defining the Standard

Working with Cary Coutant, Daveed Vandevoorde, and engineers from many companies, we created the first common C++ ABI (Application Binary Interface) for Itanium.

Impact: Though called the "Itanium C++ ABI," it was quickly adopted by GCC and other compilers for many platforms. It remains the standard to this day for new C++ revisions.

First Native Itanium Compilers

Built the first native Itanium C and C++ compilers, coordinating work of 16 different teams with 16 different ways of writing makefiles. HP's original plan was to run PA-RISC cross compilers in a PA-RISC emulator!

title: HPVM - Enterprise Virtualization
content:
Enterprise-Grade Virtualization for Itanium

HP Integrity Virtual Machines (HPVM) is a virtualization solution for Itanium-based servers. This was the longest project of my professional life (10 years) and the most complex—an enterprise-grade virtualization solution for Itanium processors.

Early Days

Started the project in late 2000 with the early help of two HP system software gurus:

  • Todd Kjos
  • Jonathan Ross

The three of us got the software to boot 4-way HP-UX guests. Then we got a much larger team of remarkably bright people, mostly former Tru64 and OpenVMS wizards.

Technical Contributions

I contributed to many facets of the product:

  • Low-level interrupt handlers
  • Binary translation
  • Memory management
  • Interrupt handling and emulation
  • Context switching (called "transmogrification" or Xmog - a Calvin and Hobbes reference)
  • Networking and disk I/O
  • Debugging tools
  • Scheduling and scalability
  • Testing
  • User-space management tools

Advanced Features

HPVM offered capabilities that are just starting to show up in open-source tools:

  • Para-virtualized I/Os
  • On-line guest migration
  • On-line addition/removal of devices, RAM, and CPUs
  • Cluster integration
  • Remarkable I/O capabilities inherited from HP-UX

Team Excellence

The team consisted of remarkably bright people, some who had been working on operating systems like TOPS-10, TOPS-20, or OpenVMS long before I knew what a calculator was. Special mention to:

  • Karen Noel - On-line guest migration, OpenVMS support, attempted to improve my OpenVMS and English skills
  • Scott Rhine - Scheduling work that gave HPVM excellent scalability

Quote: "At HP he was sought after as one of their top visionaries" - Dale Morris

title: Informagie - Science Fiction Novel
content:
A 32-Year Writing Journey

Informagie is a novel I started writing as a student, around the same time I was developing Alpha Waves. I finished it after 32 years and published it.

Story

A humorous science-fiction auto-biography by Antoine Ravelin, explaining how a video game saves humanity with the help of dinosaurs.

Features

  • Unionized green mice
  • A robotic vacuum cleaner that can tell you if the woman of your life is a cyborg
  • A psychopath antivirus gone allergic
  • A chlorophyl-based Internet where spam occupies the vast majority of Canada's forests

Language

Written in French. Working on an English translation, tentatively named "Nin, Binary," but this is super-low priority in the grand scheme of things.

Philosophy

This kind of thing makes me laugh. I hope it will make you laugh too.

title: Make-It-Quick Build System
content:
A Quick Way to Write Makefiles

Make-It-Quick is a simple build system designed to make it easy to build C or C++ programs without lengthy makefiles or the complexity of tools like automake or cmake.

Features

Simple & Readable:

  • Very short and readable makefiles
  • Offering all the most useful features
  • Compact size (~500 lines of active makefile code)

Fast: Since short makefiles with few rules are quickly parsed.

Automatic Features:

  • Incremental project configuration
  • Generates config.h file
  • Detailed build command logging in log files
  • Single-pass generation of header-file dependencies

Built-in Capabilities:

  • Product testing with make test
  • Product installation with make install
  • Compact, colorized progress report
  • Summary of errors and warnings at end of build
  • Colorization of error and warning messages

Flexible Build Modes:

  • Rules to build various targets (optimized, debug, release, profile)
  • Rule modifiers for common build options (e.g., v-debug for verbose debug)
  • Personal preferences easily defined with environment variables

Developer-Friendly:

  • Built-in help (make help)
  • Pure make, allowing standard Makefile syntax and features
  • Supports parallel builds
  • Supports separate libraries to accelerate builds

Portable: Tested on Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms.

Philosophy

Well suited for relatively small programs, though it has been used for at least one much larger program. The goal is simplicity without sacrificing power.

title: Physics Research & Books
content:
Unifying General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics

As an amateur physicist, I've long been very interested in quantum mechanics and relativity.

Theory of Incomplete Measurements

A long-sought and improbable solution to the problem of unifying quantum mechanics and general relativity.

Core Principle: A new principle of relativity suggesting we should be able to do physics using any instrument, including a broken voltmeter or watching through foggy glasses.

New Mathematics: We must learn a new way to do physics:

  • Without equations or real numbers
  • No continuum, no space, no time
  • Only discrete measurements of space and time
  • Measurements not all equivalent to one another
  • New changes of reference frame for non-linear or irreversible conversions

Probavectors: Digital pictures record the probability of detecting photons and predict the probability for a screen to emit them—the functional equivalent of a wave function, but in discrete form.

560 pages - Available for free download or purchase

Réunifions la Physique (Let's Reunify Physics)

A short, easy-to-read essay describing the theory of incomplete measurements in French.

Content:

  • Insights on rationale and history behind the theory
  • How it differs from quantum mechanics and relativity
  • Where it makes different predictions
  • Where these predictions happen to be exact

250 pages - Available for free download or purchase

Philosophy

Delusional enough to believe that I found how to unify general relativity and quantum mechanics. Whether that's true or not, the journey of exploring these ideas has been fascinating.

Related Work: Also published thoughts on special relativity as "a matter of perspective," understanding that special relativity is just regular laws of perspective in a space-time where you need to put a minus sign in the Pythagorean theorem.

title: Recorder - Flight Recorder
content:
A Lock-Free Flight Recorder for C/C++

A lock-free, real-time flight recorder for your C or C++ programs.

Features

Continuous Recording: Records information about your program continuously while it's running using simple printf-like statements.

Smart Classification: Classify recorded data in different categories to preserve both:

  • Old important events
  • Recent, rapidly-firing events

On-Demand Dumping: Dump recorded data on demand, notably in response to signals or from debugger.

Selective Tracing: Trace specific categories of records (print them as they happen).

Real-Time Visualization: Export specific data to shared memory channels for external visualization. Includes a simple Qt5.9-based visualization tool showing content of data channels in real-time.

Use Cases

Perfect for debugging complex, time-sensitive systems where traditional debugging would alter timing behavior:

  • Real-time systems
  • High-performance servers
  • Embedded systems
  • Multithreaded applications
  • Race condition debugging

Philosophy

Like an aircraft flight recorder, it's always running, capturing everything, so when something goes wrong, you have the data you need to understand what happened.

title: XL, Tao3D & ELFE
content:
An Extensible Language Journey

A 30+ year research project in programming language design, evolving through multiple iterations to create truly extensible languages.

LX - Language Expérimental (1988-1998)

Started during a training period at Alsys SA (Ada compilers), leading to reflections about what I liked and didn't like in Ada. Features included:

  • User-accessible representation for the parse tree
  • Basic garbage collection
  • Advanced generics (similar to C++ templates)

XL - From Experimental to Extensible

Following discussions with brilliant engineers like Daveed Vandevoorde, the focus changed from "experimental" to "extensible". Key evolution:

  • XL - Advanced generics, still syntax-directed
  • XL2 - Complete rewrite with simplified parse tree (8 node types), bootstrapped compiler
  • XLR - Extensible Language Runtime, designed as back-end for XL2, became elegant standalone

Tao3D - 3D Interactive Programming

A programming language for interactive 3D derived from XLR, making it easy to create great visualizations and animations quickly. Powerful enough to present complex information entertainingly.

Features:

  • Real-time 3D rendering
  • Very short code for complex animations
  • Used for talks, trade shows, museums, education
  • Commercial version by Taodyne added stereoscopy support

ELFE - Extensible Language for Everyday

The most recent evolution: a simple, small language for everyday programming, specifically tuned for IoT device configuration and control. First language to incorporate a type system based on tree shapes.

In many ways, ELFE is the best implementation of XL to date.

Quote: "Advanced and revolutionary stuff" - Raphaël Manfredi on Tao3D
